Now, I don't know the tab number, I can have them called to know screen, but if you prefer to find them among your bundle of documents please go ahead and do so. Sorry, I did, didn't? Sorry, I meant socialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was wondering whether I had heard you say, because I was sure I did hear you say, "soviet." At the same time, I was wondering where you got this from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we float off into different worlds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm conscious of the fact, Mr. Ristivojevic, that you have come here as somebody whose expertise is in the laws of the former Yugoslavia and the republics that were formed after its dissolution. But would it also be correct to say that particularly when we are looking at the International Laws of War, that is an area of law you have also studied and with which you are very familiar?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say that this is a field of my scientific interest. This is one of the topics of the International Criminal Law, but as I've already said, it is a rather unthankful thing to speak of one's self. I cannot be the judge of my own ability or expertise. It's really not up to me to talk about myself and what I can do or what I can't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's deal with a few basics in relation to these regulations. These regulations that were used not only by the Yugoslavia national army but also adopted by the armies of each of the independent republics that were formed after its dissolution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Yugoslavia broke up, whether these rules were applied in all the republics and all of the militaries, I've never checked. However, what from I know about the ways the state were building their new legal systems after the breakup of Yugoslavia, I can say with a high degree of certainty that the assumption is correct. Why am I so certain? I am certain because such a good and well-elaborated document on the application of the international law did not exist elsewhere; and all the states were interested in applying these documents. They were duty-bound to implement them, to adopt them; and instead of coming up with something new from scratch, I am sure that they decided to adopt what already existed and was good on top of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And as far as your study of these regulations is concerned, they are and were consist with the International Laws of War as you understand them to be?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very outset, the regulations explicitly says that and lists the international law sources. It says according to the Rules of the International Laws of War in terms of this document, there will be the laws ratified by the SFRY, the International Laws of War, and the international customs of war. This document was drafted with the goal of adopting very complex forms of international law and adapt them to the -- for the use in the army and also to classify all these documents and put them together in one place so as to provide for an -- for their easier use in an armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I suggest to you that the purpose of them for the army was to -- was twofold. Firstly, to inform them when they were breaking the rules, and secondly to inform them when the rules afforded them no protection. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may also be one of the purposes. It's only natural that if somebody is duty-bound to familiarise themselves with the rules that they should also be able to draw some conclusions as to what punishment could arise if they don't comply with such rules. When such rules protect them. When, on the other hand, they don't offer them any protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I am going to take you through a handful of the rules, if I may, starting with Rule 48, paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in e-court, that's B/C/S page 24 and English page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Ristivojevic, whether you're reading it in the folder or if you're reading it on the screen, but if you're reading on the screen, I think that you have it now. And it reads so that it's in the record: "A citizen who during an armed attack or a military operation in preparation for an attack wears no identification marks and cannot be distinguished from the civilian population shall be considered a competent and a member of the armed forces on condition that he openly bears arms during the military engagement." And that would have been a provision known to anybody who had been trained in the Yugoslavia national army, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So any army operating within that territory in 1995, which was comprised partly of those in military uniform and partly of those not in military uniform but bearing arms would know that those who were not in military uniform were not protected by the International Laws of War?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wonder if my colleague might rephrase the question. It seems a bit ambiguous as it's put, and that's predicated upon the condition that's indicated in sub-division 4 that he just read, "not openly bearing arms."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can phrase questions very elegantly, I'm sure. And he gets the right to cross-examine after me so he can tie it up as he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If you have difficulty understanding the question, then please say so, Mr. Ristivojevic. If you can proceed with answering the question do so by all means, otherwise, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the gentleman to repeat the question because a lot has been said in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The question I put was that -- so an army operating in one of the republics of the former Yugoslavia in 1995 which comprised forces which were partly in combat outfits and those who were in civilian clothes would know that those civilians who were bearing arms were not afforded the protection of the International Laws of War under this regulation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to these rules on the condition that somebody knows them that extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move now to point 54 which is on the B/C/S page 25 and English page 25. In fact, I think we probably need to look at Article 53 first which describes the protection afforded at the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Article 53 sets you out, doesn't it, the protection afforded the civilian population under the rules in -- in military combat, and thereafter Article 54 sets out the exceptions to that protection. And I would like to look, please, at the three specific exceptions, afforded -- the three specific exceptions to that protection listed under Article 54; namely one, if the civilian population is in a military facility; if a person who falls within the category of a civilian population is with a military unit; and three, if the civilian population is in any way in the immediate vicinity of a military facility during combat operations against such a facility.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is. Item 53 or Article 53 sets out the rule and Article 54 sets out the exceptions in that rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so that we understand what Article 54 means, we may have to go to Article 71 which is at B/C/S page 29 and English page 30. So could we do so, please. And Article 71 says: "The concept of military facility. A military facility in the meaning of the provisions of these instructions shall be understood to mean any facility which by its character, location, purpose, or use effectively contributes to military action ..." et cetera, et cetera. And you are familiar with that provision, are you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that presumably would cover a houses being used as a defensive position by military forces, would it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is used -- used as a Defence position, I would say the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or even more so, a hospital with fighters or artillery units within its ground?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in such a case combat activities should proceed with a lot more caution. However, if a hospital were to be used or abused in this way, then one could say yes to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we're coming on to that in a minute. It would also include, wouldn't it, communications facilities within buildings or any operational facility within a house or a building or anything like that? Those would all be military facilities, as you understand them within the meaning of these rules?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. However, before that, one should establish whether the facility or the house has indeed been used in combat operation and that its either partial or complete destruction would destroy its military purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come on to Article 72 please, now. Which is at B/C/S page 30 and English page 31. And just the first bullet point: "Allowed attack. Direct attacks on and bombardment of military facilities alone is allowed. Before launching an attack, it is necessary to determine whether the facility to be attacked has been identified as a military facility." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you say that that objective achieved by the obtaining of target maps which illustrate where the military facilities lay in any urban area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying the -- or asking, rather, whether a target map would be a good way to identify valuable targets? According to Article 72, before launching an attack, it is necessary to determine whether the facility to be attacked has been identified as a military facility. This could be one of the ways. I am sure that this could serve to determine whether such a facility is, indeed, a military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly, drawing all these regulations together, would those trained within these rules who placed military facilities either as it were within civilian buildings or next to a civilian population, be knowingly placing those people outside the international rules of war as described by this set of regulations?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, if a target is not a military target per se, if a facility is not a military target it cannot come under attack as a rule. However, in practice things happen; hence, paragraphs 2 and 3 that speak about the vicinity of military facility, the civilian population; and it provides guidance as to how such a military facility should be attacked. Any attack should be proportionate to the significance of the military facility. If an attack would incur major losses among the civilians, then such an attack would be contrary to the Rules of the International Laws of War. But the estimate of that would be a complex exercise that would depend on a number of factual factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different area now, which is Article 213, which is at B/C/S page 57 and English page 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's really the second sentence of the first paragraph that I'm interested in, please, Mr. Ristivojevic which reads in the English: "When capturing a member of the enemy armed forces, the commanding officer of a unit of the SFRY armed forces shall take all precautionary measures for the security of the unit."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what para 2 of item 213 reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so that we are clear the unit referred to in Article 213 is the unit commanded by the commanding officers; in other words the commander is under an absolute obligation to ensure his own units are safe and secure when taking prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let me give you another factual situation. Against the backdrop of enemy soldiers doing everything they could to avoid capture, including detonating explosives resulting in the death and injury of his soldiers, it would be consistent with a commander's duty under that article that he gave an order that nothing should be risked in the taking of prisoners, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to para 2 he is bound to undertake all precautionary measures. However, it does not specify which measures it involves, it just says "all measures." So if it is left up to the commanding officers, let's say a sort of the discretion with regard to the selection of the measures that he will employ. But I -- repeating again, there is no specific measures mentioned here as the ones being obligatory to employ or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I put as it were the factual situation in this case to you, the commander is alleged to have given an order that nothing should be risked in the taking of prisoners against that factual backdrop. Would you agree that that does not offend and is consistent with his duty under Article 213 to safeguard the security of his units?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That no risks must be taken? Well, perhaps, it could be construed in that way that all precautionary measures as paragraph 2 reads could mean that. Which means that no risks must be taken, take, all steps or undertake all measures to secure that. That's what I would assume would this hypothetical order would instruct. So if no risks are to be taken, then all precautionary measures have to be undertaken, and in that case I think that would be consistent with Article 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can leave that behind us now and move earlier in the regulations to Article 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which for those operating the e-court system is at B/C/S page 16 and English page 15. Thank you. I think we all have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am not going to read all this out to you, I am sure you are very familiar with it Mr. Ristivojevic. It's effectively creates two responsibilities on A, I'm an officer, firstly one to prevent crimes which he knew or could have known were about to be committed. And secondly, to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings against offenders who have committed offences. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less that would be the summary of Article 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It -- in order to comply with the first of those two duties, you would have to have knowledge that something was going to happen and fail to prevent it at a time when it was still possible according to the regulation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read this rule. If he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals are planning the commission of such violations, and here it refers to the violations of the International Laws of War, at the time when it was possible to prevent their commission, failed to take measures to prevent such violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could we now have in e-court 7D717, English pages 2 to 3 and B/C/S pages 6 to 7. We need to see Article 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so that you know and everybody knows what it is, this is the regulations regarding the brigade commander's authority in the regiment of 1965. This article reads: "In the absence of the commander the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander stand in for him with all the commander's rights and duties." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Article 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the situation where the commander is absent, do you understand that regulation to mean that the Chief of Staff also has the duty to prevent any crime being comitted under Article 21 that we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 17 says, "with all the commander's rights and duties," including inter alia the ones specified in Article 21. So this falls under the category of the duties referred to previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so in this situation where the Chief of Staff in the absence of the commander came into the possession of knowledge that crimes were about to be comitted, the duty would fall upon him and only him at the time that he came into that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided that he acted in compliance with the rights and duties of a commander, I would say that in that case this refers to him as well, I mean, Article 21, because he exercises all his rights and duties including the duty to undertake measures to prevent violations of the International Laws of War that were in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now come on to as it were the second limb Article 21, the duty to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings against an offender.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've already given evidence about this, and I'm not going to go over old ground unnecessarily; but there is a distinction between what acts would call for disciplinary measures and what acts would call for criminal proceedings. And if we were concerned with a solitary act of murder, for example, there would be no question that that called for disciplinary proceedings. It would call for a criminal investigation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, of course. Any violation of the laws of war stipulated under these regulations are not all within the range of serious violations. There are violations that are not serious and a disciplinary responsibility would be more appropriate. But this, of course, this what you mentioned without question would fall under serious violation; and it would entail criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we just clear up one thing, and that is the question of the establishment of special military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we would need to put into e-court at this stage 4D525, at English pages 2 to 3 and B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you and perhaps all of us to consider firstly Articles 8 and 9 and then Article 13, please, of these regulations. Article 8 states that: "A court-martial may be convened during a state of war to try criminal acts as defined under Article 9 of this law ..." And then we can go to Article 9 and sees that it says: "Pursuant to Article 8 of that law, a court-martial shall try military personnel from a military units whose officer has convened the course as well as other persons caught in the zone of responsibility of the said unit for criminal acts against the army of Republika Srpska, specifically for: Failure and refusal to carry out an order, opposing a superior officer, defection and surrender to the enemy, failure to discharge one's duty ..." And then we can go over the page and see the conclusion of that regulation: "Wilful abandonment of duty, abandonment of a position, weakening combat morale, attack on a service member." Okay. Can we now go over the page and see Article 13, please, which sets out the solitary pair of sentence under these regulations. And Article 13: "The sentence of a court-martial for special wartime situations may only be the death penalty ..." Now, just so we are clear about this, a special court-martial has no application to the situation where a commander discovers -- or might discover that crimes have been comitted towards enemy prisoners, does it? I mean, it's got nothing to do with that at all.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on the Application of the Military Courts in wartime do not have any specific explicit provision in that sense. It is possible that one of the other provisions sets it out broadly; but, however, there is no explicit mention of that. If we go to the top of the page to Article 9 here, second paragraph is the only one which allows for a possibility to draw a conclusion within the broad context on the jurisdiction of military courts over such criminal acts, inter alia. But as I say, we need an interpretation. Primary courts were devised to try criminal acts committed against the army of Republika Srpska, and we have seen the list of these criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the purpose of this set of regulations is to permit a commander in wartime to summarily execute those who commit acts of what might be called treason, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you call "acts of treason" and how you understand that. In legal science, we only construe that as an attack on the constitution order, but this is just a definition. This is not a specific criminal act. This law and these court-martials are primarily oriented towards those perpetrators whose acts are directed against the army of Republika Srpska. So there is a possibility to construe the last sentence of Article 9 in such a way to include into the jurisdiction of this course the acts that you mentioned, but I say again that would require a much broader interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I am simply trying to narrow down what it is the commander should do upon discovery of a criminal offence; for example, murder, and I was doing suggest to you that disciplinary proceedings are simply out of the question. And even if they had been created under these regulations, the special military courts have no jurisdiction unless the murderer were one of his own forces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the last thing that you mentioned, any disciplinary proceedings would be totally inappropriate in the case of murder. And an officer cannot initiate [Realtime transcript read in error, "finish"] criminal proceedings. He can just propose that procedure to be followed. The only thing that he can do is to report what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I believe that I really need to intervene because on page 58, line 20, it says "cannot finish criminal proceedings," it says "initiate." That's what witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Very pertinent remark. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, that was very helpful indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so that we are clear, you haven't specifically gone over this, but you deal with it as it were the legal requirements of the commander to investigate crime at paragraphs 5.6 to 5.8 of your report, Which we'll see at B/C/S pages 39 to 40 and English pages 41 to 43. And it might be helpful if you and we just reminded ourselves what you had to say there.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about item 5.6 of my report, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Items 5.6 to 5.8 please, Mr. Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is this last obligation mentioned under item 21 of the rules on application of Law on International Laws of War in the SFRY armed forces. What I wanted to explain was how criminal responsibility is generated and how it becomes the result of this violation. Since Item 21 does not establish criminal responsibility itself. It just establishes the duty, whereas it’s up to the criminal law to define the criminal responsibility. Specifically that would be Article 199, failure to report a crime, from the former Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was at the time called the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, parts from Article, I think, 185 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska – special part, which is the former Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So here I was explaining what that concept means, it was so to speak a crime that was common to the whole territory of the former SFRY and in all the laws later on you can –- I’m sorry, I’m sorry. So what I wanted to explain was how this criminal responsibility looks like, how a report should be made. It should be either oral or writing. It is completely irrelevant. The law also does not stipulate or prescribe any other subsequent form of a criminal report. Another thing that the law lays down is that it did not establish clear distinction between the organs who are responsible for receiving this report. When the law was drafted, nobody had commanding officers, military officers, in mind. The law was drafted and designed for a man in the street. The average man would just go to the police and report a crime. Isn’t that right? This is –- this is normal, regardless of the fact that the proceedings are really the jurisdiction of the prosecutor, isn’t that right? So the legislator's assumption was that an average person didn't know which organ is responsible for dealing with it. So he doesn't know whether he is reporting to the competent or incompetent organ. It is up to the organs to take care of that, that if a citizen reported a crime to a body that was not competent, forward it to the competent body. Therefore, the criminal code did not specify either the form of the report or the body responsible or having jurisdiction to receive it. In the event --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to leave that to one side for a moment. And go, please, if I may to paragraph 3.19 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's at pages 16 both I think in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And remind you there of the provisions within the Rules of Service of the Security Organ that you set out, paragraph 51 to 56. Tell us, please, Mr. Ristivojevic, when you've got them in front of you and you've familiarised yourself with them.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Within the structure of a brigade of the army of Republika Srpska, the responsibility for the investigation of criminal acts fell with which organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were discussing the Law on Military Courts, we said that the powers of the MUP and its members, according to the Law on Military Courts and the proceedings conducted by them, shall be taken over by security organs and the military police, each in their respective scopes of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we can look in particular at Article 52 where it reads: "When there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a criminal act within the security organs competence has been committed, authorised superior officers of the security organs are obliged to take measures that the perpetrator of the criminal act is found and the perpetrator or the accomplice does not go into hiding or escape." And in Article 53: "On the basis of the information gathered, superiors officers of security organ of the army command, Territorial Defence staff, the security organs, superior officers equal or superior to them --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "-- shall submit a criminal complaint to the competent military Prosecution office." Does it follow from that that howsoever the security organ come to know about the commission of a crime, they have a duty and an obligation to investigate it and ensure that the perpetrator does not go into hiding or escape?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might say that it has these powers stipulated in Article 52, but this is not yet strictly speaking an investigation. Therefore, there was no decision taken to launch an investigation pursuant to Law on Criminal Procedure, strictly speaking an investigation, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But the power to do that does not derive from any order of the commander of the brigade, does it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it doesn't follow. Just like the police without any previous order would do the same tasks in proceedings before the regular courts, they don’t need any specific orders, if they learn about the commission of a crime, to respond, so the security organs, or the military police, again as the law says, each within its respective jurisdiction, do not need a special order for a crime they are aware of to investigate it, to establish what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one mall intervention. In the transcript it's on page 62, line 8. The witness was referring to regular courts and regular situations, because here it says, "vis-a-vis courts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If Mr. Lazarevic says it's so, I dare say it is; but we ought to check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, do you agree with Mr. Lazarevic's clarification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So to give a concrete example, in the circumstances where a brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [French spoken on English channel] I am receiving French translation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So am I -- so are we, rather, because I've checked. I think it's a question of wrongly pushed button.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In the circumstances where the chief of security of a brigade comes to know of the possible commission of a crime, it's his duty under these rules to investigate it, irrespective of any order of his brigade commander; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it arises as a logical conclusion of what I've said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, in fact, it goes further than that, his brigade commander cannot, in fact, order him not to investigate a crime because he has a duty to investigate it under the rules?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he were to receive an order that was not legal, any member of the armed forces, pursuant to Article 239 of the criminal code of Republika Srpska, may refuse to obey such an order. Because according to the Law on the Army, nobody is duty-bound to carry out an illegal order. When we are talking about the criminal code, we have to talk about an order of the superior, it can be the basis for exclusion but not in the case when an order is illegal. Whoever receives an illegal order is duty-bound to refuse such an order. Let me go back to your question. Any illegal order anybody receives that person should not -- or must, rather, not carry that order out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then can we go back, please, to the duty of the commander to report crime as set out by you in paragraphs 5.6 to 5.8 of your report. Within the context of an army brigade, if a commander of the brigade discovers that a crime has been committed, his duty is primarily to report it to his chief of security. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say yes to that. The proper place where to report any crime should certainly be a military prosecutor. However, the criminal code does not strictly name the addressee of such a report. It is possible to report such a case to a body which is not strictly competent and still comply with the reporting application. In practice, this is what normally happens. A layperson does not know much about law and competences and when they learn about a crime, they will first go to the police rather than to the Prosecutor. We could draw a rough parallel between these two cases. So a commander of a unit relays the information about the crime to his security organ or his military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But you mention in your report at paragraphs 5.6 to 5.8, that that duty will cease to exist in circumstances where there is an objective reason for not complying with it. Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold on just a second. No. This is what I've just said. I did not change anything there. There is an obligation in the criminal code, and is binding for every citizen, and it may be considered as complied with if a crime is reported to anybody, anybody, for various reasons which may be subjective or objective. The legislator did not want to encumber a crime with many elements because he started from the assumption that the reporting obligation applies to everybody across the board, primarily a layperson, a common citizen. I've provided both examples that may be -- become part of the situation under the criminal code but the reasons are not important, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, there is a set of circumstances I'd like you to consider which is within the context of a brigade commander discovering of the commission of a crime in which his own chief of security and perhaps his professional superior were involved. Along what routes would you say he should report those matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that Mr. Ristivojevic has already told us on several occasions that he is not familiar with the military rules and that he's not military expert. He has repeated that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, having heard this, Mr. Haynes, do you wish to proceed with your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me this is the very substance of his report. Paragraphs 5.6 to 5.8 are about this very topic, I'm simply inviting him to consider a factual situation and apply paragraphs 5.6 to 5.8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ristivojevic, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I understand the logical loop that Mr. Haynes is putting me in with his hypothetical question. The person who should investigate such a crime is allegedly, as you say, involved in that crime. I believe that the legislator never envisaged such a possibility. Thus the articles 199 of the criminal code of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, and the similar one in the criminal code of Bosnia and Herzegovina do not provide for such a situation. The state will never start from the assumption that it will be the police or the Prosecutor who commit crimes, so there is nobody to report crimes to. I would say that the law does not provide any solutions in such a case. In my view, this would be a factual matter rather than a legal matter. It is very difficult to say who would be the addressee of such a report in such a case. My answer would be that the criminal code that was in effect at the time did not envisage or regulate such a matter. I will agree with you that it would be only logical to think along your ways, and it's absurd if the example that you have provided is really absurd because the perpetrator of the crime is the one who should deal with the crime and punish the crime. However, the legislator never envisaged such a situation and that's why he did not regulate it. I would have to give it a second thought, and I would have to see how the obligation might be fulfilled in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put a situation to you. Might it be fulfilled by the brigade commander informing his superior officer, the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I personally, if I were in such a situation, I would certainly talk to somebody, because the perpetrator of such a crime who in normal circumstances should be prosecuting crimes also has to be reported. If a -- the crime involves a person who should fight crime -- should also be reported. And since he is the first reporting person and he is out of the question, you have to report to somebody else. In any case, you would have to report to somebody. That would be my interpretation of the law or the requirements under the law binding the person who discovers that a crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to be difficult, Mr. Ristivojevic, but we've all taken law examines in this room, and we've all had to apply the law to factual situations. And you're here as an expert to give us your opinion, and I am going to put that question to you one more time: In the circumstances where a brigade commander feels he cannot report to matter to his chief of security because his chief of security might be implicated in the commission of crime, would he fulfill his duty under disclosure of defence of Yugoslavia law by report the matter to his superior officer, the corps commander? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I believe that that might be the case. Based on what I've said previously, I believe that in this way the disclosure obligation would be complied with; but in that case not only the crime should be reported but also the subordinate who is implicated in the commission of such a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Ms. Nikolic, you've had time to --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good evening to you and Your Honours. I do have a few questions I would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, last time you gave us an indication of 15 minutes or something like that. So yes, we'll proceed now until we have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hoping that you will finish by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good evening to you, Professor Ristivojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution I am going to put some questions to you in relation of your direct-examination and also some of your cross-examination. If I ask you something that's unclear to you please let me know, and I'll try to rephrase it in a way that you can better understand what I am driving at, all right. Now, you can see, don't you, throughout your testimony that the international standards with respect to the treatment of prisoners, such as the Geneva Conventions, apply in the circumstances that you evaluated for the purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The international laws on -- of war say that they are based on the provisions of the international law, i.e., the international treats that the former SFRY had ratified. In other words, this document on the application of the rules does not establish any new rules or obligations, but rather just adopt the international rules and present them to a foot soldier in a way that they might understand. So my answer to you would be yes, of course they are applicable, even if they did not exist. Still the former state of Yugoslavia would have been duty-bound by the international laws because that state had ratified all the Geneva Conventions and protocols.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And in preparing your report, you prepared it with specific regard to the charges that have been brought against Mr. Borovcanin in this indictment, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say that my task was also to check and provide my opinion as to what the legal position of the commander was, if he was resubordinated to a unit of the army Republika Srpska in combat. And, as we know, Mr. Borovcanin was such a police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And the conclusions that you drew in your report were drawn having that in mind, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in evaluating the international laws that apply to the particular circumstances that you looked at or addressed in your report, you, of course, recognise the authority of this court to apply the Geneva Conventions in evaluating or -- evaluating the circumstances with which Mr. Borovcanin is charged, the crimes with which he's been charged?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is not in dispute, anyway, in my report -- the report. This is not the subject of my evaluation at all. I was just tasked with analysing the national law or provide my expert opinion on the domestic law, i.e., the national laws and provisions of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it is the case, is it not, even in your report that the national laws of the Republika Srpska by expressly, and certainly if not by implication, apply the International Rules of Law, right? I am sorry for that, I just don't see an answer in the record. Maybe I can re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting. There is no answer to be recorded. I was waiting. If I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. It's my fault. Let me re-phrase it. It is the case that the laws of the Republika Srpska that you evaluated, incorporate, by reference, the international rules and laws of war, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So by definition in evaluating the domestic rules as you did in your report you necessarily evaluated the application of the international rules, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the largest extent one could say "yes" to that, but I would also have to say that there are some minor discrepancies between the domestic roles and the international laws, and that is due to the fact that the former Yugoslavia, when adopting international rules and when prescribing its own documents, sometimes it would go a step further from the international laws or went in a different direction. However, in principle my answer to your question could be "yes." What I'm saying is that the laws were not copied word for word. You will find some differences. And of course the international law regulates only certain things leaving national legislator to elaborate certain obligations. In principle the former state of Yugoslavia was up to date in that area, and the state that inherited its laws adopted them to the full, because they did not have either the time or resources to draft their own laws, especially during the war. That's why they adopted fully almost to the letter, the laws that were applied in the former state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Let me just go back to a brief point because I am not sure that I got your answer. You don't actually dispute the authority of this Tribunal to apply the Geneva Conventions in evaluating the crimes with which Mr. Borovcanin's been charged, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the application of international laws, it is the case that the domestic laws call for their application specifically under the Law of Internal Affairs; that's correct, isn't it? And in particular, I mean, I can put it up on e-court if you need to see it, but in particular I am referring to the obligations that are imposed on officials of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on Article 35, which calls for upholding, as it were, the constitutional order of the Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what were you referring to specifically? Yes. Yes. You are talking about Article 35, the last paragraph and the oath that an official has to take, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. All right. And that calls for that official or any authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to up hold the constitutional order, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's also repeated, in effect, in Article 36 where it calls upon authorised officials to perform tasks and duties aimed at protecting the constitutional order, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know that under the constitution of the Republika Srpska under Article 5 that defines the constitutional order, amongst other things, as protection of ethnic groups and other minorities and also guaranteeing and protecting -- the guarantee and protection of human rights with respect to international standards, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Most constitutions incorporate provisions of that sort, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And all of these obligations with respect to the implementation of international standards that apply in the law of the -- Law of the Ministry of Internal Affairs applies in peacetime and in wartime equally, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be more precise. You say all these standards, is that what you said? Could you please maybe rephrase or be a bit more precise when putting that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. The standards that require officials in the ministry to observe international standards and the discharge of their duties apply equally in peacetime and in times of war and in threat of war, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. However, the word, "standard" that you're using is rather broad and not very specific, and that's why I'm saying that whenever it comes to drafting legislation and respecting certain norms, international standards have to be defined, precisely defined. The Law on the Application of International Laws are the consequence of precisely such an approach. In other words, the legislator of the former SFRY, in his intent to make the Geneva Conventions more approachable or accessible to the members of the armed forces, came up with a form that was more understandable, more clear to everybody. Whenever you have something wide-ranging and broad, you have to narrow it down to very concrete and specific norms to make it more easily understandable by all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, the norms that I am referring to in particular are contained in the regulations on the application of International Laws of War and the armed forces of the Socialist Federalist Republic of Yugoslavia, that's P409. And in particular, tell me if you need me to put this up on the e-court, and I will. In particular, under sub-6 -- I'm sorry, my mistake, under sub-9, it details international treaties and other legal documents in the domains of the law of wars which the SFRY has ratified and recognized. And there are a number of them, 20 as I see in this particular document. Those are the standards to which I am referring. And do you agree that those particular standards are what are referred to within the constitutional order of the Law on the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Law on the Implementation of the Law on Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that these are international agreements that the former SFRY had ratified. I found them binding. In other words, they became binding laws in the state binding upon all of its citizens. Irrespective of whether a person is a member of the police or not, they would be bound by these norms. They didn't even have to belong to the police to be bound by these norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the case of Mr. Borovcanin in particular, those rules would be binding on him in his capacity as a -- an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs whether he's resubordinated to the VRS or not, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an authorised official, according to Article 35, is involved in discharging tasks of state and public security, then the set of authorities binding upon him are of one kind. When they are subordinated to a VRS unit, in other words, when they are engaged in combat, then they lose some of their obligations but not all of them. It is impossible to claim that somebody only because they have lost the status of an authorised official are no longer duty-bound to respect the life and health of a prisoner of war which he is obliged to respect according to the Geneva Conventions. If we go down to a lower level and talk about members of the Ministry of the Interior performing tasks and duties, and when we are talking about individual roles what makes the authorities of an authorised official, since we are talking about the tasks and duties of public and state security, when they are given combat tasks, they no longer have to perform those tasks and duties. And that is why the amount of authority changes in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs. It is only natural that one who is engaged in combat can no longer perform tasks and duties of public and state security, but this does not imply - and I agree with you in that - that that person is no longer bound by the international laws and the provisions thereof. Such a conclusion would be completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you would agree, would you not, that under Article 2 of the implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs during imminent threat of war or state of war, under that particular article, the provision of the Law on Internal Affairs and other laws on regulations in the domain of interior affairs, apply unless they are specifically exempted in that law; that is, any obligations Mr. Borovcanin would have had under the Law on Internal Affairs will continue to apply in the case of imminent threat of war or a state of war unless that law, the latter, specifically cancels out his prior obligation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree, but you used the word "specifically." The law says unless otherwise provided in the law. As I understand Article 13 of this law, it stipulates what the units subordinated to the VRS are going to do. They will be engaged in combat operation, ergo, that cannot be involved in the duties of public and state security. These two things are incompatible. The law needn’t specify everything explicitly. So, this power exists, this –- automatically, this one doesn’t exist. I mean, if you pass a legal instrument on one and the same thing, later on it naturally supersedes the earlier ones, isn’t it so? Here you have a law regulating internal affairs during an imminent threat of war –- state of war which stipulates in Chapter 4 the use of police units in combat operations. In order to use them, the logical interpretation of this law would be that you cannot use them for public or state security. What other solution could you arrive at in practice? If you have a policeman assigned to a duty, in combat would have to put down his arms and go back to his regular police work and say, I don't want to fight. He has no choice. He has no option. He simply, one set of powers is taken away in order for him to get other powers, which in my humble opinion are much more unfavourable, 21 because he can get killed in combat, whereas the chance of his getting killed on state public security business is less. I think it would be -- it would not be a good interpretation of the law on, Article 13 that the powers remain together, so, at the moment someone is assigned tasks in combat, the interpretation of the law that one and the other power remain together. I think that would not be a good interpretation of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have, probably, I think five or ten minutes. So maybe if -- if you would like, we can break or I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I let you go beyond the time because I thought you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was closing in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- finishing. So we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can continue, of course, if it is all right with everybody else, it really doesn't clash with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it's better if we break, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I am going to have some redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, I was going to ask you whether you had planned a redirect. So we'll have a 25-minute break now, and we'll continue afterwards. In the meantime, please, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Zivanovic, and Madam Fauveau, if you could meet for five minutes outside and decide exactly how you wish to proceed. We are at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 6.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good evening again, Mr. Ristivojevic. Where we left off --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where we left off, I was talking about the law concerning the implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs, and we were talking about Article 2. Now, it's not your position is it that that law, the Law on Implementing the Law on Internal Affairs at a time of war, it's no your position that that law some how supplants Mr. Borovcanin's obligations under the Law of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to abide by international standards including the Geneva Conventions, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is that international law norms are binding to a state and its citizens, provided they accept them by ratifying an international agreement. And that is speaking in principle. However, if we start speaking about specifics, then an individual normal can be observed by a citizen whereas another citizen is not in a position to do so. For example, everyone taking part in combat regardless of their rank and the unit they belong to, is by all means duty-bound to spare the life of a prisoner and to treat him humanely. There shouldn't be any difference. If we are to go into detail diminution of the application of these norms, we would arrive at a conclusion that some men could abide it and some couldn't. If we speak about Article 20, point 24, we can see that only senior officers can impose punishments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, I am not asking about punishment or anything like that, I just want to know whether it is your position that as the Law on the Implementation of the law regarding the Ministry of Internal Affairs applies during a time of war or threat of war, I want to know whether it's your position that that law supplants any obligation that Mr. Borovcanin might otherwise have had to abide by international standards and, in particular, Geneva Conventions? That's all. Is it your position that he doesn't have to abide by the it Geneva Conventions under that law or that he does?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot state that this law, in any way, and in principle, gives a right to any member of the police not to observe the provisions of the International Laws of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, let me ask you, I think I can bring this to a little bit more to reality. In a situation where you have a MUP commander of a unit that is resubordinated, as you say, pursuant to this July 10 order, resubordinated to the VRS. In a situation where he is present at a location where there are prisoners of war, where his units are stationed throughout the area, the immediate vicinity of that facility, where he has at his disposal the resources and the men to address a situation concerning those prisoners; and he's aware that those prisoners have been killed in some instances and injured in other instances. And there is a fair number of them that he, himself, actually observes. Doesn't he have an obligation to stop what is transpiring under the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I had an opportunity a couple of days ago to answer a similar question, specifically, whether Article 21 of the Rules on the Implementation of the Laws of War binds a commander of a police unit resubordinated to the VRS. And the answer I gave then is that it is my 21 opinion that is binding with regard to his subordinates, which is to say that he is obliged to undertake measures to prevent the commission of acts that are being prepared. I also said that it was my opinion, even it is not explicitly written out in Article 21, that it is a logical consequence that 25 he is obliged to prevent acts that are occurring and after that, a consequent 1 obligation that he is obliged to report if he learns subsequently, at a later point, of a crime, to report them, as Article 21 says, to the competent military officer. So this is -- this stems from the international law. This is not any -- in any way an outcome of resourcefulness and ingenious of our local legislators. It just stems from the international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Wouldn't he under circumstances where he's aware that killing is in progress be under an obligation to stop that from occurring?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what I said a minute ago. The primary obligation is if he knows that his subordinates are preparing to commit crimes, he should undertake measures to prevent them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The opinion of an expert witness about an ultimate issue, I believe it's improper in our view, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to determine, based on all the facts, whether there is some sort of responsibility of Mr. Borovcanin and not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's an entirely appropriate question given this witness's stated area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway. No harm is done. He's answered it already, and to us it was a pertinent question; however, we do wish to make it clear that his answer does not bind the Trial Chamber, ultimately, when it comes to international criminal law it is us who will decide and that doesn't necessarily depend on what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. As long as that is clear, let's proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. He's already answered. I thought I was stopping him in time, but I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate that. I hadn't noticed it in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Wouldn't that obligation also extend to stopping other individuals that are engaged in killing or other conduct detrimental to the welfare of prisoners as well? Wouldn't he have an obligation to stop that conduct as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, item 21 that we are talking about, was originally designed for military officers as its title indicates. We are now talking about a different kind of commander. We are talking about a police commander who, unlike military officer, has no rank which is a necessary prerequisite for him to be able to discharge duties of a military commander. Secondly, he doesn't have the powers of a military commander. Once we reach this point, I believe that what needs to be taken into account when we interpret item 1 -- 21, and the duties of a police commander. Although he it doesn't say here explicitly a police commander, this is just a basis for our conclusions relating to a police commander, what should be relevant and taken into account is the amount of powers which should be in correlation with one's duties. What does that mean? That means that if a commander has powers to issue orders to his subordinates, my opinion is that he has obligation concerning conduct of these subordinates. Unlike a police commander, an army commander issues orders to his subordinate but also to other people who are not. According to Rules of Service of the VRS, I think in item 17, says that he issues orders to his subordinates, and in the absence of a superior, the most senior officer issues orders and everyone is obliged to carry them out. As for a police commander, the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on Internal Affairs during an imminent threat of war or a state of war. I was unable to find this kind of powers vested in the police commander in terms of issuing orders to the individuals who are not subordinate to him. Therefore, my opinion is that the amount of powers is the criterion that should correlate and correspond to the duties. If a person can issue orders to others then he should be responsible for those orders and for these men. As for the men that he cannot issue orders to, he cannot assume any responsibility for their conduct. I have resorted to this interpretation because I repeat item 21 speaks about military officers not police officers. This served only as a basis for drawing a conclusion about the duties of a police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could show you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could we have 4D371 in e-court, please. I think it's page 2 on the B/C/S. And what I want to direct your attention to is item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see it yet, but I'll read it into the record --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just scroll down a bit. And the next page in B/C/S, please, if it's no problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what this document is an order on the application of the Rules of International Laws of War in the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, right? And in item 2, it refers to commanders of all units as well as each member of the army or other armed formation, and takes place in combat activities are responsible for the application of the Rules of the International Law of War, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would apply to Mr. Borovcanin, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about item 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Item 2.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 says that commanders of all military units as well as each member of the army or other armed formation who takes part in combat activities are responsible for the application of the Rules of the International Laws of War. This is a provision laid down in principle, meaning that everyone participating in an armed conflict are bound by the International Laws of War. If we move on further, then we can find different examples of the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That applies to Mr. Borovcanin, in other words, right? In his capacity as a MUP commander of a unit that is resubordinated to the VRS in July 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, as I already stated, is that a commander of a police unit is bound by the rules vis-a-vis his subordinates in the way I already explained. Once we come to specific rules, differences emerge. Everyone is bound to spare the life of a prisoner. There is no difference in that respect. However, it differs when we speak about different ranks and different people in the army and the police and how the rules apply to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we have P409 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am going to refer you to Article 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's page 15 in the English. Just a moment, I'll get you the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This has already been read into the record but, I just wanted you to have an opportunity to see it. And what it describes in point 21 is the responsibility for the actions of the subordinates and it says: "An officer shall be personally liable for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that you units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violation ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we discussed this item 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. And that speaks to the responsibility, of Mr. Borovcanin in this particular instance, as concerns units other than units subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a statement or question, I apologise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's a question.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered that, but I will repeat. My view is as follows: This document was drafted in 1988 when the police was not part of the armed forces. And he then took into account those powers that commanders in the army and in the Territorial Defence, and they have ranks too, and they are soldiers too, have with regard to their subordinates, and then I quote other units or individuals’. Now we are faced with another situation. So now we are faced with a different situation in which we have a commander of a different formation which is not part of the military, has also become an integral part of the armed forces, and can be used in combat activities. We cannot, if we apply purely linguistic interpretation, apply this normal to him. If you read military officer, then it would mean that it cannot apply to it. However, we had two different types of commanders in combat, ones who were bound to take care of their subordinates and the others who were not. Now, we have to find a way of how to interpret this norm in order to apply to the commanders of other units. What I said last week, and I said 15 minutes ago and I'm going to say it again, the principle and the criterion to be adhered to with regards to the obligations inherent in this article to the unit which is not a military unit, should be functional; and it should stipulate what his powers are and what kind of obligations stem from these powers. This was meant for military officers, who, I repeat, under the rules of military service, can issue orders both to their subordinates and those who are not. I will refer you to Article 17 of the Provisional Rules on -- 1 of Rules of Service of the VRS, provisional from 1992, Article 17 which says, issues orders first to his subordinates but then the most senior ranking officer and to all others, regardless of whether they are his subordinates or not’. So the military officer for whom this is meant. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I think we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I would like to know what the witness says. We haven't receives interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't hold this against me. I have already said this two or three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have an issue with the translation of this document. In English version of Article 21 of paragraph 21 it says: "An officer shall be personally liable," and also it refers to an officer in the second paragraph of this item. But in B/C/S version, it says: "Military officer." So just in order to avoid any confusion, I think that the witness can read first sentence and the first sentence of the second paragraph just to make sure we are talking about military officer, because this refers to military officer. And he was talking about linguistic understanding, that's what he was referring about. He was having B/C/S text in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness can tell us whether he answered the question on the basis of the B/C/S version that he has in front of him or whether he was referring to the English text, because if he was referring to the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no problem. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have in e-court, please, P28. Okay. I just want to have the first page up if we could, so we can see what it is; and then I'll refer you to the page I am looking for. This is a Main Staff order dated 6 October 1992, concerning the guidelines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to see this document in preparing your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what it refers to are guidelines for determining criminal prosecution, and it is prepared by the military prosecutor's office at the Main Staff of the armed forces, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just go one page over in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not give me an opportunity to answer. You said "right?" And then I did not get a chance to answer, may I? According to this version that I have in front of me, the list that one receives is in handwriting and some of it is part of the body of the text. First of all I can see that it says, "guidelines for criminal Prosecution and the criteria thereof." When we look at the purpose of this document in the second paragraph of the heading, it says in order to unify the criteria of the evelation [as interpreted] of certain crimes and prosecution of the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I -- stop, stop, stop. Please, listen to me. The interpreters are having problems. You are reading too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What am I saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One portion of witness's answer was not recorded. And he said, "I cannot see by looking at this document that it's an order." This is what I heard him saying, and I cannot see this in the transcript, so maybe he can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am not surprised at this so because he was going too fast. So I don't expect the interpreters to work miracles here, especially at 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All I want to know, Mr. Ristivojevic, is have you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- before?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you seen this prior to and during the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all I want to know. If I could refer you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer, Mr. Vanderpuye, and you, Mr. Lazarevic, how long do you expect your redirect to last? I would like to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is basically my last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's not waste more time or lose more time. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could go to page 8 in the English and page 29 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29? There is no 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said page 29, and that page does not exist in the guidelines. The guidelines finish with the age -- with the page 17. You misspoke when you said the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
