utterances.text: 17 in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17 does exist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Then I understand that it might be 13.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 13 in front of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then the version on e-court is one page shy of where it needs to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go one page forward in the e-court English version, I think I can -- page 9, I think I will be where I need to. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I have in e-court now is part of the section that relates to the offences against humanity and international law pursuant to chapter 16 of the criminal code, and what it reads is as follows, what I want to direct your attention to: "From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders in command of the armed forces whose members could commit or are committing some of these offences to take uncompromising action and to prevent such conduct. This responsibility belongs by its nature, particularly, to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military, or public organisations who are in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders. If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves, and expose perpetrators to criminal Prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for those criminal offences." In your analysis of this particular provisions, these particular guidelines, it is the case that this would apply directly to the conduct of Mr. Borovcanin as is charged in this indictment; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the following: This legal document, by its legal nature, is just a declaration. It does not establish any legal rights and obligations. Its aim is to provide the guidelines to the legislator as to what the elements of the crimes are in more specific terms so as to allow the legislator to unify the crime prevention and prosecution policies. This is nothing new. It is just a repetition of what is already inherent in the criminal law and other documents. So this does not establish new rights, obligations that do not exist in the legal order. It is a mere declaration of what already exists in the legal order. In my view, what is said in here, what you've just read out, does not differ from Article 21 that we have already discussed and that I have already interpreted in my own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm afraid you haven't answered my question, and my question is: You say that these are guidelines that refer to concrete rules, and my question is does that apply to Mr. Borovcanin as he found himself in the circumstances in July 1995? That's my question, and you can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my opinion guidelines are of a declarative nature. They do not create any legal obligations and they don't give rights to anybody, including Mr. Borovcanin. They just declare what already exists, they are nothing new. They were drafted with an intention to list the elements of criminal acts in order to allow the military judiciary to unify their Prosecution policies. So this is nothing new. This speaks of the already-existing law and the existing crimes that exist in chapter 16. This is an interpretation by the supreme prosecutor of Republika Srpska. His interpretation of the existing law of the Chapter 16 of the criminal code and other legal documents. Do you understand what I'm saying? He is speaking about the existing law. He does not establish any new rights and obligations. This is just like an order by the president of the republic that he issued in 1992 on the obligation to respect the International Laws of War. This is nothing new. This is just a declaration to remind everybody of the obligation to respect the rules and laws of war. And particularly issued to members of the military and others involved in combat. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, as I said earlier, we are the ones who are going to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the legal effects --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- of such a directive, whether it's a directive or an order and what responsibilities, domestically and internationally may be attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My question wasn't to repeat this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to do ask you, sir, was you referred earlier to Mr. Borovcanin's obligations with respect to the conduct of other individuals who may not have been subordinated to him or other military units. You are not suggesting, certainly, by your answer that if he's aware of the commission of crimes by those units, even if they are not subordinated to him or under his control, that in his presence he has no obligation to intervene and no obligation to stop patently and obviously illegal conduct towards prisoners of war? You are not suggesting that, are you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV RISTIVOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. What I've told you so far, this is what I claim with regard to the obligations of an officer according to item 21 and my interpretation thereof. In this particular concrete situation that you have just proposed, the criminal code of the former SFRY, in the chapter on crimes against body and limb, there is a crime that could be applied to this situation that you are talking about. This is a failure to extend assistance. Whoever is in a position to extend assistance to a person whose life is in danger, without putting his own life in jeopardy or another person's in jeopardy, if they fail to do so, they would be taken to prison. So there was a punishment for that. A crime which was called "Failure to Extend Assistance." What I'm saying is that the situation that you are talking about is to a certain extent covered by the criminal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristivojevic. I have your answer. Thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Regrettably, I am going to need at least 30 minutes, maybe more, because I have a number of documents. However, I was informed that Mr. Ristivojevic flight is scheduled for tomorrow afternoon, so I think I will be able to finish in 30, 40 minutes. My colleague has extended his time significantly as was indicated which puts me in a situation that I really cannot finish with my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we have -- sound antagonistic in any way, Mr. Lazarevic, provided we keep within reasonable time. Shall we start now or do you prefer to start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would really like if we can start tomorrow, that would give me the opportunity to go through this, maybe I can even streamline my cross-examination once I go through today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. That's why I have asked you, because I am hopeful that you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. We are sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. What time is his flight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half past 5.00. He should make it. If we start at 2.15 and finish in 30 minutes, then he should make it. All right. We'll give you 30 minutes, not a minute more unless you find -- you show us good cause, Mr. Lazarevic. Have your things prepared, packed, and ready, so that you will leave straight from the airport from here as soon as you finish your testimony. Thank you. We stand adjourned.
